content: A study on the capacity of countries to address non-communicable diseases (NCDs) globally could investigate several critical aspects. These include whether government funding is allocated for pediatric palliative care (PPC), whether a national policy exists that incorporates PPC, and whether pediatric policies include palliative care provisions. It would also examine whether these policies are operational, under development, or not yet implemented. Additionally, the study could assess the availability of oral morphine in more than 50% of inpatient and outpatient pediatric care facilities within the public health sector, as well as the accessibility of palliative care to over 50% of pediatric patients in the public health system. Furthermore, it would evaluate whether palliative home care services are accessible to more than 50% of pediatric patients in the public health system. The World Health Organization (WHO) supports the use of health technology assessments (HTAs) to systematically evaluate the properties, effects, and impacts of health interventions. HTAs consider both the direct, intended consequences of interventions and their indirect, unintended effects. This approach is instrumental in informing policy and decision-making in healthcare, particularly in determining the optimal allocation of limited resources for health interventions. HTAs are conducted by interdisciplinary teams using explicit analytical frameworks, drawing on clinical, epidemiological, health economic, and other relevant data and methodologies. HTAs can be applied to various interventions, such as including home care in public health insurance coverage, implementing broad public health programs like palliative care, setting priorities in healthcare, identifying health interventions that yield the greatest health benefits and cost-effectiveness, and developing clinical guidelines. Providers of pediatric palliative care, regardless of the care setting, must commit to continuously improving the quality of their services. Data collected from quality indicators serve as a primary source of information for enhancing these services. A basic framework for indicators to assess key domains of national or regional programs has been described and adapted from a previous WHO guide for planning managers. In fragile states, HTAs can define essential services, emergency kits, and disaster planning. In low-income countries with low coverage, HTAs can define primary healthcare packages. In middle-income countries with low coverage, HTAs can define guaranteed packages of care. In countries with strong health systems, HTAs can employ marginal analysis to determine additions to existing care packages. This continuum of HTA activities supports health systems in planning and implementing effective interventions. Sample indicators for assessing improved access to pediatric palliative care in primary healthcare include the existence of a national pediatric strategy or plan that incorporates palliative care, the inclusion of an essential package of pediatric palliative care and symptom relief in universal health coverage, and the presence of laws and regulations for safe and effective opioid prescribing in line with international drug conventions. Other indicators include the proportion of medical, nursing, and technical schools that include pediatric palliative care education in their undergraduate curricula, the inclusion of pediatric palliative care on the official list of services provided at the primary care level, and the availability of essential medicines for palliative care, such as oral morphine, in primary healthcare settings. Outcome indicators include the percentage of pediatric patients who had access to palliative care at the time of death and the percentage of deceased patients who received pediatric palliative care. These indicators are adapted from WHO guidelines and other key studies to ensure comprehensive evaluation and integration of palliative care into pediatric healthcare systems.
